A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TFPS research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial supplementary expansion and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting experiments on eight datasets, component ablations, and expert analyses, including Tables 2–3 and Figures 4–8.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds Traffic evaluation, additional baseline comparisons, parameter searches, targeted ablations, and efficiency measurements.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Algorithm 1 retain the dual-domain encoders, subspace clustering, expert routing, aggregation, and training objective. Newly specified initialization and parameter values clarify implementation without establishing a changed procedure. Alternative architectures are evaluated as ablations, while Wasserstein distance replaces a diagnostic metric.

E1.justification: v2 adds Traffic, containing hourly road occupancy from 862 sensors, to the original eight datasets (Table 1 and Appendix A). This adds a transportation domain while retaining the same multivariate forecasting task and all previous dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated comparisons with AutoTimes, Moment, Timer, MoLE, MoU, KAN4TSF, Koopa, SOLID, and OneNet. It also adds DLinear combined with SIN, SAN, Dish-TS, and RevIN. Within the retained FEDformer normalization comparison, NST is removed from v1 Table 6 to v2 Table 8; the other four normalization methods remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds separate evaluations searching input lengths over 96, 192, 336, and 512, plus systematic regularization-weight sweeps and controlled component replacements (Appendices F, J, and K). Shift diagnostics in Figures 1 and 8 and Table 5 change from MMD to Wasserstein distance. The original benchmark splits, forecasting horizons, and fixed input lengths remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablation, v2 tests imaginary Fourier components, branch-specific PI removal, R1/R2 removal, and alternatives to MoPE. It adds alpha/beta sensitivity, t-SNE representations, expert-allocation distributions, and efficiency analysis. The expert-count analysis changes its second dataset from ETTh2 to Weather, and clustering diagnostics are revised using Wasserstein distance.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, uncertainty intervals, error bars, or significance tests for its experiments. The added checklist marks statistical significance as NA but supplies no new statistical reporting.

E6.justification: The main-table forecasting values for the original eight datasets are unchanged. v2 adds Traffic results, including TFPS MSE values 0.427, 0.445, 0.459, and 0.496 across the four horizons, and extensive tuned, additional-baseline, ablation, and efficiency results. Wasserstein measurements replace MMD diagnostics. Results obtained through input-length search are additional settings, not demonstrated same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: v1 Appendix B's MMD definition, RKHS derivation, and empirical estimator are replaced by the Wasserstein transport definition and CDF equivalence in v2 Appendix C. This changes the mathematical basis of the diagnostics. The principal TFPS equations remain unchanged, and no new original theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains forecasting through dual-domain representations, subspace clustering, and pattern-specific experts. The abstract changes its highlighted performance claim from particular strength in long-term forecasting to particular strength on datasets exhibiting significant distribution shifts, a limited refocusing of the advertised advantage.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for weaker foundation-model comparisons on Traffic, reduced advantages after input-length tuning, regularization sensitivity, real-only Fourier processing, and expert-allocation behavior. It revises the expert-count interpretation around Weather and Wasserstein distances and introduces efficiency tradeoff claims. The existing limitations concerning heuristic patch lengths and emerging patterns are retained.

D1.justification: v2 specifies eta = d, Gaussian initialization of subspace bases, q = C × D, d = q/K, and a recommended beta near 0.1. It adds implementation provenance for foundation-model comparisons and a Traffic data-source link. These extend documentation; the repository link, optimizer, GPU, embedding dimension, and encoder depth were already disclosed.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning around foundation models, specialized expert models, and distribution shifts, adding references such as AutoTimes, Moment, Timer, MoLE, OneNet, DUET, and Mixmamba. The earlier Time-LLM/MOIRAI discussion explaining exclusion of pretrained models disappears. Existing time-frequency and general MoE discussions are largely retained or relocated.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites portions of the abstract and motivation, condenses the PI explanation, moves time-frequency related work into the appendix, and reorganizes existing supplementary material into dedicated comparison and analysis sections. It also adds a conference checklist and funding section. This constitutes substantial document restructuring despite considerable retained method prose.

P2.justification: v2 expands and reorganizes the comparison tables, adds numerous ablation and efficiency tables, and introduces t-SNE, expert-allocation, and sensitivity plots in Figures 9–11. Shift heatmaps and expert-count charts are revised, alongside conference formatting changes. Figure 6(b) retains an ETTh2 label despite the accompanying Weather discussion.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct comparisons with specialized MoE and distribution-shift competitors and isolated tests of several central design choices. v2 addresses these gaps through Tables 10–11 and 13–16, supported by input-length-search comparisons and additional implementation details. This substantially strengthens validation of the contribution. Reporting defects temper the gain: Appendix I claims a speed advantage over PatchTST, whereas Table 12 reports 6.114 versus 4.861 ms, and uncertainty remains unreported. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvement in experimental support.
